a: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. It emphasizes readability with its clean syntax and indentation-based code blocks. Python is dynamically typed (no variable type declarations), garbage-collected, and supports multiple paradigms: procedural, object-oriented, and functional. Key features include a comprehensive standard library (batteries included), large ecosystem of third-party packages (PyPI has over 400,000 packages), and strong community support. Python dominates in data science (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn), machine learning (TensorFlow, PyTorch), artificial intelligence, web development (Django, Flask), automation, and scientific computing. It is widely used in education for teaching programming fundamentals. Python is open-source, runs on all major platforms, and has excellent interoperability with C/C++ through extensions. Version 3 (released 2008) is the current standard; Python 2 was retired in 2020.

JavaScript (JS) is a high-level, interpreted programming language primarily used for web development. Created by Brendan Eich in 1995 at Netscape, it was standardized as ECMAScript. JavaScript is the core technology of the World Wide Web alongside HTML and CSS, enabling client-side interactivity in browsers. It supports event-driven, functional, and object-oriented programming styles. Key features include dynamic typing, first-class functions, prototypes-based inheritance (ES6 introduced classes), asynchronous programming (callbacks, Promises, async/await), and the Document Object Model (DOM) API for manipulating web pages. The language has evolved significantly: ES6 (2015) introduced let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules, and template literals. Node.js (2009) extended JavaScript to server-side programming. Major frameworks include React (UI components, Facebook), Angular (application framework, Google), Vue.js (progressive framework), and Next.js (React-based full-stack). JavaScript is also used in mobile development (React Native), desktop apps (Electron), and cloud functions.

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing relational databases. Developed at IBM in the 1970s and standardized by ANSI and ISO, SQL allows users to create, read, update, and delete data. Key commands include SELECT (retrieve data), INSERT (add new rows), UPDATE (modify existing data), DELETE (remove rows), CREATE TABLE (define new tables), ALTER TABLE (modify table structure), and DROP TABLE (delete tables). SELECT statements can include WHERE (filter rows), JOIN (combine data from multiple tables: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL), GROUP BY (aggregate data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN), ORDER BY (sort results), and HAVING (filter aggregated data). Subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs) enable complex queries. Database indexes speed up searches. Transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) ensure data integrity. ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantee reliable transactions. Major SQL databases include MySQL, PostgreSQL (advanced open-source), SQLite (embedded), Microsoft SQL Server, and Oracle Database. NoSQL databases (MongoDB, Cassandra, Redis) offer alternatives for specific use cases.

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, developed by Facebook (now Meta) and released in 2013. React is component-based: UIs are built from independent, reusable pieces (components) that manage their own state. Components use JSX (JavaScript XML), a syntax extension that combines HTML-like markup with JavaScript logic. Key concepts include props (input data passed to components), state (internal component data), hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext, useReducer — allowing state management in functional components), and the virtual DOM (a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM that React uses to efficiently update the browser, minimizing expensive DOM manipulations). React follows a unidirectional data flow (data passes from parent to child components). Server-side rendering is supported through Next.js and Gatsby. React Native extends React to mobile app development. Major companies using React include Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, Airbnb, and Uber. React's ecosystem includes state management libraries (Redux, Zustand), routing (React Router), and testing tools (Jest, React Testing Library). React's popularity stems from its simplicity, performance, and vast community.

Git is a distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for Linux kernel development. It tracks changes to files over time, enabling multiple developers to collaborate. Git is distributed — every developer has a complete copy of the repository history. Key concepts include repositories (project folders with .git tracking directory), commits (snapshots of changes with unique SHA-1 hashes), branches (independent lines of development, enabling parallel work), and remotes (remote repository copies, like GitHub). Basic workflow: git init (initialize repo), git add (stage changes), git commit (save staged changes with a message), git push (send commits to remote), git pull (fetch and merge remote changes). Branching commands: git branch (list/create branches), git checkout (switch branches), git merge (combine branches), git rebase (reapply commits on top of another branch). Collaboration typically uses feature branches (created for each feature), pull requests (code review before merging), and merge/pull strategies. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are popular hosting platforms. Git's advantages include offline work, branching/merging efficiency, data integrity (SHA-1 hashing), and speed.
